name: Eric Liddell
title: Eric Liddell: life went on after the medal
description: Olympic champion in Paris and teacher in China, Eric Liddell left a story of conviction, teaching, and care during wartime.

sections.heading: A conviction in the middle of competition
paragraphs: Eric Liddell was born in China in 1902, the son of Scottish missionaries. He studied in Britain and excelled in sports. At the 1924 Paris Olympic Games he won the gold medal in the 400 meters, after giving up the 100 meters because of his conviction about Sunday.

That decision usually takes center stage in how the public remembers him. Yet his life went on far from the podium. He returned to China to work as a teacher and missionary. Everyday service, teaching students, and family responsibilities filled the years after his athletic fame.

sections.heading: Serving when life became hard
paragraphs: In 1943 he was interned by Japanese forces in the Weihsien camp. There he helped organize activities, taught, and stood by other prisoners. The organization that preserves his legacy has gathered memories from people who shared that experience with him.

Liddell died in February 1945, before the camp was liberated. Accounts of how he treated children and adults broaden the picture of the champion. His story lets us see a faithfulness that also showed itself in small tasks, in circumstances he had not chosen.

reflection: Hebrews 12:1–3 uses the image of a race to speak of perseverance and turns our eyes toward Jesus. The image helps us rethink what we call success. Everyday obedience can include learning, working well, and standing by someone without those actions receiving public recognition.

Liddell’s medal does not set up a promise of athletic victory for anyone who keeps their convictions. Faith also goes through losses. We can learn from his care for others in the internment camp and look for a concrete task of service in the circumstances we live in today.
review_note: Dialogue from Chariots of Fire is not used as historical quotation. The Olympic victory is not presented as a reward promised for obedience.
source_labels: The Eric Liddell Community. “About Eric Liddell,” biography and memories of fellow internees.
